author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(288): one total order for queue position, display, and admission

CodeRabbit round 1 on PR #98, both findings.

MAJOR (#271). `enqueued_at` alone is a PARTIAL order — SQLite stores it as
RFC3339 text and Postgres stamps NOW(), so two requests in the same tick tie —
and the three consumers disagreed about what to do with a tie.
`list_scan_queue` sorted on (enqueued_at, user_did) but counted position as
`enqueued_at <=`, so tied rows rendered 1st/2nd/3rd while all of them were
told they were 3rd. `scan_queue_entry` repeated the same count.
`claim_next_scan` ordered on enqueued_at alone, so the row actually admitted
was not necessarily the row the dashboard showed as next — the display order
and the admission order were different orders.

All five queries across both backends now use (enqueued_at, user_did): a
row-value comparison for the two position predicates, the same pair in both
ORDER BYs. Row values rather than an OR expansion so the predicate is visibly
the same expression the ORDER BY sorts on — two spellings of one order is how
they drift apart again.

Four regression tests, one per backend surface plus the equivalence itself.
They seed rows sharing ONE enqueued_at written directly to the table, because
`enqueue_scan` stamps wall-clock time and its rows cannot tie, and insert them
in reverse user_did order so rowid/heap order is the exact reverse of the
expected answer. Verified red first: all three positions came back 3, and
admission took the row displayed LAST. The Postgres claim assertion was never
reached in that red run, so it got its own negative control — reverting only
that ORDER BY makes it fail and nothing else.

MINOR. The admin dashboard carried a failed scan's reason solely in a `title`
attribute on a non-focusable span: unreachable by keyboard, unannounced by
screen readers, absent entirely on touch. The cell now renders the reason
inline under "Failed", shortened to 72 chars so a RunPod payload cannot widen
the 9rem column, with the full untruncated phrase in a visually-hidden sibling
and the visible copy aria-hidden. No new literal colour, font-size, or radius:
--charcoal-400 (the AA floor for body text here) and 0.8125rem, both already
in the file.

Closes #271.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(288): give the wedged-queue alert a dwell before it fires

Running this locally is what found it. The bare condition -- queued > 0
while running < cap -- is routinely true during entirely healthy
operation, so alerting on it instantly would put a red "scans stopped
happening" banner on the page several times an hour.

Two ways it goes true without anything being wrong: a row that reaches
the table without going through enqueue_scan never fires the try_send
wake and simply waits for the next tick, and a slot that frees is
briefly idle before the next claim commits.

Measured against a local server with three rows inserted directly:
bare-condition TRUE at t=0s and t=8s, cleared by t=16s when the tick
claimed them. An alert with no dwell fires for that whole window.

TICK is 30s server-side (admitter.rs:53), so the alert now requires the
condition to persist past 45s -- margin for a slow claim, without hiding
a real stall for meaningfully longer. The timestamp is captured on the
transition into the condition and cleared on the way out, so the dwell
measures the stall itself rather than how long the page happened to be
open.

Refs #288, #286

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(288): show the scan queue on the admin dashboard

The admin page could not see the queue. Its only scan column came from
the process-local ScanManager, which knows nothing about queued work,
loses everything on restart, and cannot see another replica -- the view
every other admission decision moved off in #257/#278. Since admin
triggers now enqueue rather than launch, an admin-triggered scan sat
queued and this page showed nothing at all about it.

Queue first: a Scan Queue section is now the first block on the page,
above Add Protected User, because "what is the system doing right now"
is the reason to open it. It carries a capacity line sourced from the
cap, and an ordered list of ACTIVE scans only -- a queue is ordered and
usually short, so one row per registered user would bury it.

The users table keeps its Last Scan column but it is status-aware now:
running shows elapsed, queued shows position, failed shows the reason,
and a user with no queue row at all reads "Never scanned" -- a
distinction the old column could not draw.

Three states this kind of panel usually gets wrong:

- Idle renders as "No scans running or queued." Plain text, no spinner.
  Idle is a real answer, not a loading state.
- Queued is described as WAITING, never as progress. PRODUCT.md makes
  that rule for the user-facing view; it applies just as much to the
  operator, who otherwise cannot tell a stalled queue from a busy one.
- A wedged queue -- rows waiting while a slot is free -- gets a visible
  alert. That is #286s silent-failure state, and until now it existed
  only as an ERROR line in a log nobody greps.

Also fixes the poll, which fired only while a fingerprint was building.
Fingerprints finish in seconds; scans run for hours, so the panel would
have rendered once and frozen.

Promotes two colours into tokens.css and DESIGN.md (#255). #f87171 and
#86efac were already shipped six times each across the authed surfaces
as bare hex -- the system HAD an error and a success colour, they just
had no name, so every file retyped them. Naming them is what let this
section use var(--) throughout: it adds no new literal colour, size or
radius, and the file now imports tokens.css for the first time (#250).

Refs #288, #255, #250, #286

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(288): show the admin dashboard the real scan queue

GET /api/admin/users built its only scan column from the process-local
ScanManager, so it knew only about scans this process launched: empty
after a redeploy, blind to a second replica, no concept of "queued" — so
an admin-triggered scan, which since #257 is enqueued rather than
launched, showed nothing at all — and unable to tell a failed scan from
one that never ran. Every other admission decision moved to the durable
scan_queue row in #257/#278; this was the last consumer left behind.

Adds Database::list_scan_queue, returning every row with the same
correlated-COUNT position that scan_queue_entry computes (two formulas
for one number is how the panel and the per-user column start
disagreeing). One query serves both consumers: the handler indexes it by
DID to enrich each user with status, position, started/finished and last
error, and filters the queued+running rows into a "queue" panel carrying
the CHARCOAL_SCAN_CONCURRENCY cap they are measured against.

last_scan_at keeps its name and its meaning — "when the most recent scan
started" — but now comes from the durable row, so it survives a restart.
fingerprint_building deliberately stays on ScanManager: it tracks a
tokio::spawn this process owns and has no durable row anywhere. A
database error fails the request rather than degrading to "nobody has
ever scanned", because an operator acts on that.

Postgres renders timestamps via to_rfc3339(), never ::TEXT, which varies
with the connection TimeZone and is not RFC3339 at all.

Tested on both backends per #270. The ordering tests seed timestamps
running BACKWARDS rather than using enqueue_scan, because NOW()-stamped
rows come back in insertion order anyway — SQLite returns rowid order and
Postgres heap order for an unordered SELECT, so the obvious version of
this test passes against a query with no ORDER BY. Verified by deleting
the clause: both backends returned insertion order and both tests caught
it.

fix(257): clear CodeRabbit PR #96 round-2 findings

Six findings, each with a test that fails without the fix.

- PublicAtpClient had no request timeout. Async reqwest has no default
  one, so a host that accepts the connection and never answers held a
  gather task forever; the #182 retries cannot help a request that never
  returns. Same 30s/10s constants as the Constellation fix (#235), and a
  regression test that takes the mock full 30s without them.
- eta_seconds differed between backends: SQLite truncated durations with
  num_seconds(), Postgres kept fractions via EXTRACT(EPOCH ...). SQLite
  now keeps the fraction — eta multiplies the median by the batch count,

  rounding both would discard precision Postgres already has. Added a
  cross-backend parity test seeded with identical timestamps.

  payload dropped, in both ScanStatus::last_error and the durable
  scan_queue row. Reuses scan_phases::panic_message, now pub(crate).

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(257): add schema v12 to backfill scan_queue.claim_id, plus review fixes

CodeRabbit round 1 on PR #96.

v11 was amended in place to add the claim_id fencing token while #257 was
still on its branch. That was reasonable — v11 had never shipped — but it is
not sufficient. Both migration runners skip a version that schema_version
already records, so a database created from the PRE-amendment v11 has a
scan_queue with no claim_id AND version 11 recorded: 0011 never runs again
and the column is never added. Every claim, heartbeat and finish then fails
with a missing-column error. Amending 0011 cannot repair that, because 0011
is exactly the migration those databases no longer run.

v12 adds the column on both backends. Postgres uses ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS
and self-records its version (the runner does not do it — a migration that
omits the INSERT re-runs forever). SQLite has no IF NOT EXISTS, so it probes
sqlite_master for the table and pragma_table_info for the column and only
ALTERs when the column is genuinely missing. On a fresh database v11 already
creates the column, so v12 is a clean no-op.

Verified both directions on both backends against live databases, including
a negative control: neutering the ALTER makes the pre-amendment test fail.
No deployed environment is affected — staging and production are both at v10
with no scan_queue table — so the exposed population is developer machines.

Also in this pass:

- POST /api/scan and the admin trigger reported position: 0 when the queue
  read-back failed, with the error discarded. 0 is a REAL position — it is
  what a running scan reports — so that made "the database read failed"
  indistinguishable from "your scan is already running". Both endpoints now
  log the error and emit position: null, which no successful read produces.
  Same silent-failure shape already fixed in delete_user.
- .impeccable/design.json component examples carried 6 transitions and 4
  hover transforms behind a single prefers-reduced-motion query, so the
  copyable examples contradicted DESIGN.md, which calls the query mandatory.
  Each animated example now guards its own motion.
- PRODUCT.md described the scan flow without the queued state this branch
  introduces, and still claimed no design system was binding. Both corrected;
  the init provenance is kept because it is worth keeping.
- Four scan_queue Postgres tests shared two DIDs. Not a live failure, but a
  load-bearing coincidence in tests whose whole purpose is isolation.

Refs #257

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(257): propagate pipeline errors, and correct three review findings

Four findings from the final whole-branch review.

I1 (src/web/scan_job.rs): run_scan passed the pipeline Result to
record_scan_outcome and then returned Ok(()) unconditionally, so
run_under_slot classified every pipeline failure as SlotExit::Completed
and finish_queued_scan wrote status=done with a NULL error. Beyond the
durable row lying to an operator, that poisoned the ETA:
scan_queue_entry medians finished_at - started_at over status=done rows,
so a scan that died two minutes in became a two-minute *successful* scan
and every queued user was quoted it. The tail of run_scan is now a
finish_scan seam that records the outcome and then returns the Result,
so the error survives.

This was the fifth instance on this branch of a test asserting a
guarantee it never exercised: a_failed_scan_releases_its_slot drives
run_under_slot with a hand-written async { Err(..) }, a shape production
never produced, since SlotExit::Failed was only reachable from the ?s in
model/classifier/fingerprint setup. The new test composes the real
finish_scan and was watched failing first (left: Completed, right:
Failed). Its ETA assertion was separately verified able to fail: under
the bug the next queued user got eta_seconds Some(0) instead of None.

Consequence of the fix: a pipeline error now reaches the Failed arm of
run_under_slot, whose generic "see server logs" line would overwrite the
more useful message record_scan_outcome wrote (partial results may have
been saved). That arm now leaves an already-Failed phase message alone;
setup errors and panics never get that far and still need one.

I2 (dashboard/+page.svelte): the header read "Scan in progress - 47m
12s" for a QUEUED user, ticking, counted from their previous scan,
because scan_running is true while queued and started_at is the
process-local ScanManager value that is never cleared when a scan
finishes. Gated on isQueued the same way line 235 already was; queued
users fall through to "Last scan: ...", which is what that timestamp
actually is.

I3 (src/web/admitter.rs):
a_lease_that_lapses_after_boot_is_still_reclaimed claimed with a 1s
lease, so a tokio::spawn delayed past that second let the BOOT pass
reclaim the row and the test silently degenerated into
boot_reclaims_before_the_first_claim - passing without exercising the
every-pass reclaim that keeps a mid-scan redeploy from wedging the
admitter. Chose the lease raise (3s, timeout 20s) as the primary fix
because it is a margin rather than a race, and ALSO added the
still-running assertion right after the spawn so a future narrowing
fails loudly instead of silently.

I5 (CHANGELOG.md): added the three shipped changes that had no entry -
models load once at boot with a fatal failure and a ~0.78 to ~1.28GB
idle RAM rise, #182 read retries, #264 Phase A timing split. Removed
three entries that were auto-generated chainlink issue TITLES rather
than descriptions of shipped code (#246 an audit, #239 a branch
integration, #262 closed as not needed). Same cleanup as fd37833.

Verified: cargo test --features web 727 passed / 0 failed / 0 SKIP;

web, postgres and no-features; npm test 36 passed; svelte-check and
eslint report no new problems in the edited file; svelte-autofixer
reports no issues.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(257): tell a queued user they are waiting, not scanning

GET /api/status has served a `queued` phase and a `queue` block since Task 6,
but the SPA had no such phase: `phaseToStepIndex` clamped it to 0, so a user
waiting for a free slot watched "Reading your posts" spin with a live elapsed
timer while nothing at all was running. The one screen that exists to tell
someone whether they are safe was telling them work was underway when it was
not.

ScanProgress now renders a distinct waiting state for `queued` — no checklist,
no progress bar, no counters, no spinner — with the position and, when there
is one, the estimate: "You're 3rd in line - about 70 minutes". The estimate is
omitted rather than defaulted when eta_seconds is null (no completed scan to
take a median from), and the copy says so out loud instead of inventing a
number. `phaseToStepIndex('queued')` returns -1 for the same reason: no step
has started.

The dashboard header drops its "Scanning..." spinner for a still "Queued"
marker on the same grounds.

Accessibility, both in the launch set for this component:

- #248: the step spinner and the bar transition are now gated behind
  prefers-reduced-motion. The waiting state adds no motion at all.
- #249: elapsed, progress message, expectation and pending-step text were
  2.3-3.6:1 on this panel and now use colors.body-text (6.9:1); the new
  waiting copy is body-text and body-text-bright (6.9:1 and 11.7:1). Step
  state is carried by icon and weight rather than by fading text below AA.
- The position line is the only aria-live region and is polite, so a 5s poll
  re-announces the position and not the whole panel.

Styling comes from tokens.css via var(), which #250 found was imported
nowhere; both edited files now import it rather than adding more literal hex.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(257): POST /api/scan queues instead of refusing

Before this, a second concurrent user got 409 "Another scan is already in
progress on this server" — under open signup (#256) that is their entire
experience, and with 22min-2h scans they could see it all day.

Now both trigger endpoints enqueue (idempotent by user_did PK), wake the
admitter so a free slot is taken immediately rather than on the next 30s
tick, and return 202 with position and ETA. The admin trigger enqueues like
everyone else per Bryan's ruling — it used to call launch_scan directly, so
its scans never touched scan_queue and real concurrency would have been
CHARCOAL_SCAN_CONCURRENCY + admin scans. One admission path, cap holds.

launch_scan is now pub(crate) and demands a QueueSlot, so there is no way
left to start a scan outside the queue. The any_running flag is deleted
outright: with the queue as the admission authority it could only disagree
with it, and did in both directions.

GET /api/status prefers the durable scan_queue row over the process-local
ScanManager, gaining a queued phase and a queue block omitted entirely when
the user is not waiting, so existing clients see no change.

Also fixes three defects that were dormant only because nothing enqueued:

#273 — run_admitter reclaims and admits in the same pass, and the oldest
queued row is usually the one it just re-queued, for a user whose pipeline
is still executing. Two pipelines then wrote the same scan_state resume
markers and both drained classification_queue against RunPod, where the $2
ceiling is per scan. Admission now consults an in-process registry of live
claims, released by a guard on every exit. Not keyed on ScanManager, whose
entry deliberately still says running — that would refuse the successor
forever. Seen RED: launched ["did:plc:live", "did:plc:live"].

#274 — run_scan writes its terminal status from inside the scan future,
before run_under_slot classifies the exit, so a zombie that finished inside
the window had already stamped Done over its successor's live entry. The
prior fix covered only the Abandoned arm, which that write never takes.
Status writes are now fenced on the owning claim_id. Seen RED.

#275 — AtCapacity drops from WARN to INFO. It fires every 30s tick while
any backlog exists, and under open signup a standing backlog is the steady
state; at WARN it trains an operator to filter the level that carries the
Wedged ERROR.

Refs #257, #273, #274, #275

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(257): reclaim lapsed leases every pass, not only at boot

The lease backstop ran once, before the admitter loop. Both backends only
reclaim rows whose lease has ALREADY lapsed, and claim_next_scan counts
every running row regardless of lease, so any row whose lease expired
after the boot pass held its slot for the life of the process — silently,
since claim_next_scan returns Ok(None) for that exactly as it does for an
empty queue.

The timeline is the ordinary redeploy: Railway starts the new container
while the old one still heartbeats, so the new boot reclaim correctly
finds nothing; the old container is then stopped and its rows freeze with
a lease that lapses a minute later with nobody watching. Scans run 22min
to 2h, so at cap 2 two redeploys wedge admission permanently.

Reclaiming in-process is safe because of the fencing token: a live but
starved worker sees Lost on its next beat and abandons.

Also in this wave:

- run_under_slot: the scan/heartbeat composition split out of launch_scan
  behind a generic future, so all four exits (Ok, Err, panic, lease lost)
  are asserted against in-memory SQLite instead of being untestable
  without ~500MB of ONNX models.
- Abandonment no longer clobbers the successor. The C1 fix makes reclaim
  reachable at runtime, at which point the zombie ScanManager write would
  overwrite a successor entry and report a running scan as failed.
- scan_queue_depth() on both backends + stall_kind(): a stall under the
  cap now logs at ERROR instead of looking identical to an idle queue.
  spawn_admitter awaits its own JoinHandle so a dead loop is loud.
- select! matches the heartbeat join result: a JoinError is the heartbeat
  TASK dying, not the lease lapsing, and now respawns instead of killing
  a two-hour scan with a false "slot was reassigned".
- HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL 40s -> 30s (LEASE_SECS/4). The comments claimed
  three beats of slack; at 40s there were two. Slack is load-bearing now
  that a lapsed lease is acted on within a tick.
- Closed wake channel cannot hot-spin (Some(()) pattern disables the
  branch instead of completing it instantly).
- Module header describes single-path admission as the target state and
  names the two paths that still bypass the cap.

Tests: +7 web (713), +2 postgres (626). The reclaim test was seen red
against the boot-only implementation, and the abandonment test red
against the clobbering one.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(257): admitter loop claims queued scans under a cap

One background task per process, and the only thing that turns a queued
row into a running scan. Wakes on enqueue, on completion, and on a 30s
backstop tick; claims while running < CHARCOAL_SCAN_CONCURRENCY (default
2, clamped 1..8).

Reclaims at boot before its first claim: any row still running when this
process starts belongs to a scan it did not start, so the lease is stale
by definition. Without it two orphaned rows deadlock a cap-2 server.

The fencing bool is now unignorable. heartbeat_scan and
finish_queued_scan return a bare Result<bool> whose bool nothing marks,
so the whole I2 property could be dropped by writing `.await?;`. Both are
wrapped in #[must_use] ClaimStatus, and every outcome is handled
distinctly: released, superseded (leave the successor alone, do not
retry), or the DB was unreachable (the slot stays held until the lease
reclaim frees it). A lost heartbeat abandons the scan rather than burning
GPU budget on a slot another worker now owns.

A scan that fails to launch releases its slot immediately rather than
holding it until the lease lapses — otherwise one bad row throttles the
whole server for two minutes.

Config is defensive: zero or garbage falls back to 2 rather than
disabling admission, which would silently stop every scan.

launch_scan gains an Option<QueueSlot>; the two direct callers pass None
until #257 Task 6 moves POST /api/scan to an enqueue. Admission logic is
tested against a ScanLauncher seam so it does not need the 500MB model
volume — 5 of the 6 behavioural tests were observed red first, and the
sixth (wake-not-tick) was negative-controlled.

Refs #257

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
docs(257): correct the spec claim that SKIP LOCKED enforced the cap

The spec asserted "concurrent enqueue never admits past the limit — the
SKIP LOCKED guarantee" and called the design multi-replica-correct. Both
were wrong, and Task 4 shipped the defect they described. SKIP LOCKED is
a safe-dequeue idiom; it says nothing about HOW MANY rows get dequeued.
The unlocked COUNT(*) in front of it is the real gate, and at READ
COMMITTED two admitters pass it together — then SKIP LOCKED hands them
different rows, so the cap breaks cleanly instead of loudly. Reproduced
at cap 1: running_after = 2. The cap is now held by pg_advisory_xact_lock
taken before the count.

Also records that the testing section needed a genuinely concurrent
claim test — sequential awaits on one connection never contend a row, so
the original passed against an implementation that over-admits.

Task 4 and Task 5 plan sections now carry warnings that their listings
are superseded: signatures changed to carry a claim/fencing token.

Separately, CLAUDE.md documented a Postgres test command that cannot
work — postgres://charcoal:charcoal@localhost fails with
FATAL: role "charcoal" does not exist, because a Homebrew install
creates a superuser named after the OS account. Every agent following
those instructions hits it (#272).

Refs #257, #272

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(257): enforce the scan admission cap under concurrency

The cap did not hold. claim_next_scan counted running rows at READ
COMMITTED, which takes no lock, so two admitters both read the same
pre-claim count, both passed the guard, and SKIP LOCKED handed them
different rows. Reproduced with four concurrent claimers at cap 1:
two were admitted. pg_advisory_xact_lock at the top of the transaction
makes admission single-file; SKIP LOCKED stays for row selection.

The old cap test could not catch this: three sequential awaits on one
connection never contend. Replaced with a JoinSet of concurrent claims,
seen RED (got 2, want 1, 3 of 3 runs) before the lock went in.

finish_queued_scan had no status guard and nothing tied it to the claim
that produced it, so a worker whose lease lapsed could stomp the new
owner row to done and free a slot still in use. Added a claim_id fencing
token, generated database-side (gen_random_uuid on Postgres,
randomblob on SQLite) so it costs no new Rust dependency. claim returns
it, heartbeat and finish require it and now return bool so a worker can
tell its claim was stolen. reclaim and re-enqueue null it out.

SQLite is not vulnerable to the admission race as wired - one
Mutex<Connection> held across the whole call - but WAL mode plus BEGIN
DEFERRED would let two processes over-admit, so the transaction is now
BEGIN IMMEDIATE and fails loudly instead.

Also: enqueued_at goes through DateTime<Utc>::to_rfc3339 so both
backends agree; ETA is None unless queued, and divides by the cap
(ceil(position / cap) * median) instead of overstating by up to the cap
factor; NULL leases are reclaimable; row errors propagate instead of
being dropped by filter_map(ok).

Schema v11 is unshipped, so the v11 migrations were amended in place
rather than adding a v12.

Test coverage the review found missing: idempotency now asserts
enqueued_at is unchanged (the row count could never have caught the
guard being removed - user_did is the primary key), FIFO claim order,
heartbeat, finish on success and failure, double-finish, stale-claim
rejection, done to re-enqueue, and NULL-lease reclaim. Both new guards
negative-controlled.

Two pre-existing harness problems surfaced: cleanup_test_data deleted a
scan_state key owned by one test from a helper six tests call, and the
scan_queue tests could not recover from a panic because cap and position
are whole-table figures. Both fixed.

Refs #257

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(257): scan_queue table and Database methods (schema v11)

Replaces ScanManager any_running bool with a durable queue. Admission
becomes "how many rows are running?" — which survives a redeploy, is
correct with more than one replica, and makes position and ETA real
rather than guessed.

user_did as PK makes enqueue idempotent, so a double-click cannot
double-book. lease_expires is what makes the deploy cadence safe: a
killed scan lapses and is re-queued at boot, and #208 scan_phase means it
resumes rather than restarts.

Postgres claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so two admitters never take
the same row. SQLite uses a write transaction — single process, no
SKIP LOCKED needed — and is deliberately minimal because #263 deletes
that backend.

Cap test negative-controlled: with the guard widened it fails on the
third claim, so it is measuring the cap rather than passing vacuously.

Also: delete_user_data (both backends) now clears scan_queue rows, and
table_count fixtures updated from 11 to 12 for the new table. The three
new Postgres tests are serialized behind a static mutex in the test file
— unlike every other table here, scan queue position/count is genuinely
global rather than user-scoped, so under the default parallel test
harness one test could observe another's in-flight queued row. Confirmed
by direct reproduction (~1 failure in 3 runs before the fix, 6/6 clean
after) rather than assumed.

Refs #257

author: Bryan Guffey

feat(257): load ONNX models once at boot into AppState

Models loaded per scan so they were not held while idle. Since #231 moved
NLI to the fp32 export that is ~500MB per concurrent scan against a
1.11GB production peak, which is what makes concurrency unsafe rather
than merely untidy — the global scan gate was implicitly protecting
memory, not just leftover from single-user days.

ScanModels holds all three behind Arc; scans clone handles. Their
existing Arc<Mutex<Session>> is untouched: this changes ownership and
lifetime, not concurrency semantics.

Fail-fast at boot rather than degrading per scan. The per-scan path
degraded when a model was absent; at boot that would hide a broken model
volume behind a green healthcheck.

Accepted cost: prod idles ~0.776GB today and ~1.28GB after, raising the
metered RAM floor (#188) even on days nobody scans.

Added a blanket impl<T: ToxicityScorer + ?Sized> ToxicityScorer for
Arc<T> (src/toxicity/traits.rs) so a shared Arc<OnnxToxicityScorer> can
be boxed as Box<dyn ToxicityScorer> for TwoStageToxicityScorer::new
without a second load or touching that constructor signature.

but tests must not require the ~500MB model volume to construct an
AppState. build_test_app[_with_db] now return Option, gated behind a

elsewhere in the suite); callers in tests/web_labels.rs and

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(264): capture Stage-1 ONNX inference time in Phase A timing split

Phase A timing (#264, e1d4fa3) missed the Stage-1 score_batch call in
stage1_outcome — real ONNX inference that runs for every account before
the Stage-2 clean pass, on the same model mutex. That made clean_pass_ms
and inference_pct systematically undercount inference share for the
#257 concurrency decision, biasing it toward looking safer to raise
concurrency than it actually is.

Adds GatherTiming.stage1_onnx_ms as a third, separately-visible bucket
(Stage 1 runs for every account; Stage 2 only for survivors, so folding
them together would blur two different questions). inference_pct() now
sums both buckets. stage1_outcome gains a stage1_outcome_timed sibling
that narrows the timer to just the scorer.score_batch(...) call --
none of stage1_outcome's non-inference work (language coverage gate,
<5-posts check, TF-IDF extraction, early-exit comparison) is included.
stage1_outcome itself is unchanged for its other callers.

Adds a wiring test (gather_account_populates_all_timing_buckets_when_reaching_stage_2)
using delayed test doubles, since no prior test asserted gather_account
actually produces non-zero timings -- only that the GatherTiming struct
arithmetic works in isolation.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
perf(264): record Phase A fetch vs clean-pass split

The #257 concurrency default rested on an estimate. An earlier draft of
the spec claimed Phase A was "~100% Bluesky I/O"; tracing the call sites
showed gather.rs runs the ONNX clean pass in the same phase, so two
concurrent scans contend on the shared model mutex by an unmeasured

should approach 2x; 30%+ means the mutex is the ceiling and the lever is
a session pool rather than more concurrency.

phase tunable.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(234): make the SQLite deletion sequence atomic

CodeRabbit on PR #93: delete_user_data ran independent conn.execute calls
with no transaction, so a failure partway through left the account
half-deleted -- scan_skips cleared while the users row survived, or the
account gone with its scanned-account DIDs and error text still on disk. For
a deletion path the partial outcome is the dangerous one.

It was also asymmetric: the Postgres backend already wrapped the same
sequence in a transaction. Production runs Postgres, so this does not change
the promotion risk -- it closes the gap for local/CLI SQLite use and makes
the two backends behave the same.

unchecked_transaction() because the fn takes &Connection; rusqlite
transaction() needs &mut, which would ripple through every caller for no
behavioural gain. CodeRabbit rated this a heavy lift assuming that
signature change was required.

Test forces a real mid-sequence failure by dropping the users table so the
final statement fails, then asserts the earlier scan_skips delete rolled
back. Without the transaction each execute autocommits, so scan_skips would
already be gone and the assertion fails -- it genuinely guards.

40 suites zero skips, 15 Postgres tests, clippy clean on all three feature
sets.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(233): stream model downloads to disk instead of buffering in RAM

download_file called response.bytes() -- despite a comment claiming it
streamed -- holding the whole artifact in memory before a blocking
std::fs::write. With the fp32 NLI model (#231) that is ~284MB resident per
download, on the async runtime.

The sharper problem was crash safety: a killed container mid-write left a
TRUNCATED file at the destination, and nli_files_present only checks
existence. A partial model.onnx would look present and then fail ONNX
parsing on every boot -- a poison state needing manual cleanup on the
volume. That risk is load-bearing for #231, whose migration story is
"existing volumes re-download themselves".

Downloads now stream chunk-by-chunk to a sibling .part file and atomically
rename into place. Sibling rather than the system temp dir so the rename
stays on one filesystem (the Railway volume); a cross-device rename would
silently degrade to a copy and reintroduce the partial-file window.

Three tests via wiremock: full body lands and the .part is cleaned up; a
failed request leaves nothing at dest; a stale .part from a killed run is
truncated rather than appended to.

Clippy clean on web/postgres/no-features; 40 suites pass, zero skips.

Closes #233

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
test(231): evaluate the fp32 NLI export on Linux x86_64

Bryan chose to evaluate fp32 before deciding how to fix #231. The fp32
export contains 144 MatMul and ZERO DynamicQuantizeLinear/MatMulInteger,
so there is no shared per-tensor activation scale for batching to perturb.

On macOS ARM64 it is exactly equivalence-preserving -- d(batch5) is
+0.000000 on all five hypotheses and pad2 matches single -- while still
running batched 1.95x faster than 5x single. It also gives the reference
values the quantized model was approximating: hypothesis 0 truth 0.131468
vs quantized 0.121953 (macOS) and 0.171669 (Linux), so the quantized model
was distorting even unbatched.

This runs the same measurement on x86_64, the platform that matters, and
times it so the inference-cost side of the trade-off is measured.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
docs(230): record the language-gate evasion trade-off at the gate (#232)

CodeRabbit flagged pair_is_assessable as an evasion lever (CWE-693): an
amplifier controls their own text, so padding an English hostile reply until
it is majority non-Latin drops the pair and forfeits the context multiplier.
Real, and #230 made it deterministic where it was previously arbitrary noise
— so in adversarial terms this is partially a regression, not purely a raised
ceiling. Recorded honestly in #232 rather than argued away.

Bounded: the multiplier is [1.0, 1.5] so at most ~33% off the threat score,
the post must be MAJORITY non-Latin (mixed-script mostly-English is not
dropped — pinned by tests/unit_language.rs), and #222 coverage_gate sends
broadly non-Latin engagement to the surfaced NotAssessed tier rather than a
quiet Low. Residue is one targeted pair on an otherwise-English account.

Not taking the suggested fix. "Score the assessable span" is not
implementable: HYPOTHESES are relational against one joint premise, so
dropping a side asks whether a text attacks the author of a text that is no
longer there, and dropping only the non-Latin characters would hand the
attacker control over which substring reaches the model. A real fix needs a
multilingual cross-encoder or abstention-as-signal — scoped in #232.

Comment only, no behavior change.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
docs(230): design spec for amplification-pair language abstention

Brainstormed design for #230. Two corrections to the issue kickoff note,
both established from the code:

- quote_toxicity (amplification.rs:117) is display-only — computed,
  printed, discarded. Never persisted, never scored. The premise that an
  English model silently scores non-English quotes as benign does not
  hold on the toxicity path.
- There are three ungated NLI seams, not two. profile.rs:686 (Mode B
  inferred pairs) was missing from the note and feeds the same
  account_scores.context_score multiplier.

Error direction is inflation, not suppression: context_multiplier is

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(toxicity): truncate over-long input instead of dropping the account (#220) The 2026-07-19 staging scan finished degraded=true with 59 accounts silently skipped. 34 of them failed with a bare "ONNX inference failed". ROOT CAUSE: Bluesky caps a post at 300 GRAPHEMES, not tokens. That is ~63 tokens of Latin ASCII but 602 in emoji, 902 in CJK, and 4202 in ZWJ family emoji — all past the 512 that unbiased-toxic-roberta accepts. onnx.rs derived max_len from the longest input in the batch with no clamp, so session.run hard-errored at the /roberta/Expand node ("invalid expand shape"). Because scoring is batched per account, ONE over-long post took the entire batch down and gather skipped the whole account. The dropped accounts were selected by SCRIPT, not at random: CJK, Cyrillic, Arabic, Devanagari and emoji-heavy text failed while Latin-script accounts passed. For a harassment detector that is a fairness gap, not just a completeness one. Note it is not purely a non-English issue — ZWJ emoji cost ~14 tokens each, so emoji-heavy English overflows too. FIX: configure the tokenizer with TruncationParams (what HuggingFace does by default), which keeps special tokens correct where a manual id-slice would drop the trailing . Direction is Left, deliberately. Replies are scored as the envelope "[Parent post]:

\n\n[Reply]: "; the default Right truncation cuts from the end and would eat THE REPLY — the text actually being judged — while preserving the parent nobody scores. Mutation-verified: with Right, a hostile and a benign reply both score 0.0012, i.e. every over-long reply silently reads as benign. ALSO: log the anyhow source chain ({e:#}) in the scan_phases error paths. Plain %e prints only the outermost .context() and drops the cause, which is the single reason this took a log dig instead of five minutes. Verified the sibling embedder does NOT share the bug (MiniLM tolerates over-long input where RoBERTa errors), so the fix does not merely relocate the crash. Covered by a regression test since the toxicity fix removes the short-circuit that was hiding that path. Tests: 6 model-gated regression tests, all mutation-checked. author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat(cost): real-time spend across concurrent RunPod workers (#185)

The ScanCostMeter modeled ONE worker (elapsed × $3.29/hr), but RunPod
bills $3.29/hr PER worker and the burst runs up to workersMax (10)
concurrently. So a multi-worker burst under-counted real spend by ~the
worker multiple: the 2026-06-26 staging resume burst estimated ~$2 while
real cost was ~$6-10. The $2 "cap" was not a real spend cap.

Replace the single-worker wall-clock with a worker-seconds INTEGRAL:
  ∫ min(in_flight, workersMax) dt
accumulated in a private `Acc` under a short (no-await) lock. Each RunPod
call arms an RAII `InFlightGuard` (enter on arm, leave on drop) so
in_flight tracks true concurrency; the integral is capped at workersMax
(extra in-flight calls queue, not bill). `estimated_cents()` and the
disaster-brake trip now read worker-seconds — the `over_ceiling`
predicate is unchanged, just fed the real quantity. New env
`CHARCOAL_RUNPOD_WORKERS_MAX` (default 10) sets the cap.

TDD: 4 Acc integral tests (single/concurrent/cap/idle), 4 meter tests
(trip/guard/disabled/real-dollar), migrated the 2 short-circuit tests to
the new force_worker_seconds seam; the 11 predicate tests are unchanged.
Full --features web suite (31 binaries) green; clippy clean
web/default/postgres.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix(burst): survive transient classifier failures, widen RunPod retries (#183)

The #178 staging scan aborted in the burst phase on a single RunPod
transport error: one ~few-second serverless blip outran the retry budget
(3 retries / ~3.5s window), and run_burst then propagated the error,
killing a 4905-item burst before finalize.

Two changes:

1. Typed transient errors + graceful burst stop. The RunPod client now
   maps a retry-exhausted *transient* error (transport / 5xx) to a typed
   ClassifierTransientError; a *permanent* error (4xx) passes through.
   run_burst downcasts to it (like CostCeilingExceeded) and returns the
   new BurstOutcome::Interrupted: successes are recorded, the rest stay
   pending, and run_phased_scan finishes degraded-but-resumable instead
   of hard-aborting. A resume retries the pending rows once the backend
   recovers. Permanent errors STILL abort — leaving such a row pending
   would livelock every resume.

2. Wider retry budget. Default max_retries 3->6 with an 8s max-delay cap
   (~20s window), so a typical RunPod scale-up / blip is absorbed by
   retries before it ever reaches the burst stop path.

TDD: 5 new tests (transient->Interrupted+resumable, permanent->abort,
error mapping for 5xx/4xx, widened default). Full --features web suite
(31 binaries) green; clippy clean web/default/postgres.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
perf(sweep): parallelize second-degree follower fetch (#178)

The second-degree sweep awaited fetch_followers one first-degree
follower at a time. On a big-account onboarding this serial network
chain is the dominant cost — the measured #207 baseline was ~2h08m
pre-burst, ~100% Bluesky I/O — even though the classifier burst is
already solved.

Replace the serial for-loop with a buffer_unordered fan-out (capped at
concurrency.clamp(1,64), matching run_gather), then fold the results
sequentially. Dedup must stay sequential (a HashSet cannot be shared
across the in-flight futures) but it is cheap; all the wall-clock was in
the awaits. The fold is extracted into a pure dedup_second_degree helper
so its order-independence — the one real risk of going concurrent, since
buffer_unordered delivers batches in arbitrary order — is unit-tested.

The produced second-degree pool is the same set as before: a follower's
profile fields are its own, so which first-degree follower we discover
them through is immaterial.

Tests: 2 new unit tests (order-independence + error-skip); full web
suite (31 binaries) green; clippy clean.

message:
fix(cope-b): poll /status when /runsync returns before completion

RunPods /runsync waits ~90s then returns the current job envelope; for a
job that has not finished (cold starts routinely exceed that), the body is

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
fix: address PR #46 round-3 CodeRabbit findings

Four findings from the third review pass. All real, all fixed.

Fixed:

- topic_search.rs (discover_by_topic error swallowing): the loop over
  keywords previously logged each `search_posts_for_authors` failure
  via `tracing::warn!` and continued. If every keyword search failed
  (e.g., AT Proto outage), the function returned `Ok(vec![])` —
  indistinguishable from a clean topic neighborhood with no matches.
  Now tracks a `successful_searches` counter and a `last_error` chain;
  if the keyword list was non-empty and zero searches succeeded, returns
  an `Err` so callers can react to the outage. Single-keyword failures
  still fall through (best-effort across the cycle).

- profile.rs (Stage 1 vacuous-pass guard): the round-2 fix excluded
  reply scores from `stage1_clean_pass_scores`, but a reply-only or
  reply-heavy sample (e.g., 1 original + 24 replies) could still pass
  vacuously because `iter().all()` returns true for empty slices and
  for tiny "all 1 entry below threshold" slices that didn't actually
  inspect the bulk of the content. Added
  `MIN_FIRST_PERSON_POSTS_FOR_EARLY_EXIT = 5` constant and a guard in
  `should_early_exit_stage1`: samples with fewer than 5 originals+quotes
  always proceed to Stage 2, where Zentropi can do pair classification
  with parent context. New tests pin both the empty-slice and the
  too-few-entries cases.

- profile.rs (graph_distance dropped on early returns): the
  "Insufficient Data" early return and the Stage 1 early-exit return
  both set `graph_distance: None`, throwing away the value the caller
  had computed. `GraphDistance` is `Copy` so the same value is reachable
  from all three return sites; both early returns now set
  `graph_distance: graph_distance.map(|d| d.as_str().to_string())`,
  matching the full-pipeline branch. Downstream consumers (sweep
  ranking, UI) preserve the signal even on insufficient-data and
  early-exit accounts.

- zentropi.rs (module-doc clarity): the doc comment didn't make clear
  that `refs/labeler_prompt.txt` is a checked-in reference snapshot
  rather than the runtime source. Added an explicit "Policy source of
  truth" section: the active policy lives on Zentropi's side,
  identified by `ZENTROPI_LABELER_ID` and pinned by
  `ZENTROPI_LABELER_VERSION_ID`; runtime behavior changes only after
  re-uploading the policy and bumping the version env var. Maintainers
  who edit the reference file should now know it has no runtime effect
  on its own.

guards). Clippy `-D warnings` clean across `--features web`,
`--features postgres`, and no-features. Rustfmt clean.

author: Bryan Guffey
message:
feat: Phase 5 — Zentropi binary classifier replaces Groq ensemble

ONNX becomes a clean-pass filter (< 0.10 = cleared); posts at or above
the threshold go to Zentropi for a binary toxic/safe verdict that drives
the threat formula's toxicity rate. Replaces the ONNX+Groq Safeguard
ensemble approach with a two-stage pipeline matching the architecture
briefing's target state.

Why: Phase 0 spike (#173) validated Zentropi at 100% accuracy / 190ms
latency. Groq Safeguard was an unsustainable-cost stopgap; Zentropi's
conversation-scoped labeler policy correctly distinguishes ally use of
identity terms from hostile use, which the ONNX model cannot.

Toxicity scoring:
- New `src/toxicity/zentropi.rs` — production `ZentropiClient` with
  10s timeout, 3-retry exponential backoff on 5xx/429/network errors,
  and a `run_diagnostic` smoke-test method.
- New `TwoStageToxicityScorer` (in `ensemble.rs`) wraps a continuous
  primary (ONNX or Perspective) with an optional Zentropi binary
  classifier. Bounded parallelism via `buffer_unordered(4)`. Falls back
  to ONNX 0.50 threshold when Zentropi is unavailable so local dev
  still works without a key.
- Added `BinaryVerdict` + `classify_batch_with_contexts` to the
  `ToxicityScorer` trait. Default impl uses a 0.50 threshold;
  `TwoStageToxicityScorer` overrides with the real two-stage pipeline.

Scoring formula:
- `build_profile` now batch-classifies with per-post parent context for
  replies (so the Zentropi labeler evaluates reply-toward-author
  hostility correctly).
- Toxicity rate = reply-weighted binary count via the existing
  `compute_reply_weighted_toxicity`. Replies count 70%, originals +
  quotes count 30%.
- Evidence ranking: surface Zentropi-flagged posts first, sorted by
  ONNX score; fall back to highest-ONNX when nothing is flagged.
- `weighted_toxicity` (the ONNX-category-weighted patch for ONNX's
  inability to distinguish intent) removed from the scoring path.

Wiring:
- `src/main.rs` and `src/web/scan_job.rs` build `TwoStageToxicityScorer`
  from a new `build_zentropi[_client]` helper. `Commands::ZentropiSpike`
  renamed to `Commands::ZentropiCheck` with neutral OK/WARN messaging

Removed:
- `src/toxicity/groq_safeguard.rs` and `groq_api_key` config field.
- `src/toxicity/zentropi_spike.rs` (promoted to `zentropi.rs`).
- `docs/superpowers/{plans,specs}/2026-03-27-groq-ensemble-scorer-*.md`.

feat: multi-user schema redesign (v0.5) (#14)

* docs: add multi-user schema redesign implementation plan

11-task plan covering schema migration v4, Database trait changes,
both backend implementations, pipeline threading, CLI DID resolution,
web handler auth extraction, and test updates.

* feat(db): add migration v4 — multi-user schema with user_did columns

Creates users table, rebuilds topic_fingerprint/account_scores/scan_state
with user_did in their primary keys, adds user_did column to
amplification_events, and rebuilds indices to include user_did.
Existing data backfilled with empty string user_did.

* feat(db): add user_did parameter to all Database trait methods

Add user_did as first parameter to every user-scoped method in the
Database trait, enabling per-user data isolation. Also add upsert_user
method for user management. table_count remains global (unscoped).

Implementations will be updated in subsequent tasks.

* feat(db): scope all SQLite queries to user_did

All 17 query functions now take user_did as a parameter to scope
data per protected user. SQL queries updated with composite key
WHERE clauses and INSERT columns. Added upsert_user() function
for the new users table. All tests updated with TEST_USER constant
and user isolation tests added.

* feat(db): update SqliteDatabase trait impl for user_did params

Forward user_did to all queries::* calls, add upsert_user method,
update all tests with TEST_USER constant, fix table_count assertion
for migration v4 (5 -> 6 tables).

* feat(db): update PgDatabase for multi-user schema

Add migration v4 (0004_multiuser.sql) that creates users table and adds
user_did column to all data tables with updated composite primary keys.

Update all PgDatabase trait method implementations to accept user_did
parameter and scope all queries per-user. Add upsert_user method.

* feat(pipeline): thread user_did through amplification, sweep, and status

* feat(cli): resolve handle to DID and thread user_did through all commands

Every CLI command that calls DB methods now:
1. Resolves config.bluesky_handle to a DID
2. Calls db.upsert_user() to ensure the user row exists
3. Passes user_did to all DB and pipeline function calls

Added resolve_and_register_user() helper. Updated load_fingerprint()
and load_embedder() to accept user_did parameter. Status command
gracefully handles missing BLUESKY_HANDLE with empty string fallback.
Migrate command registers user in both source and target databases.

* feat(web): extract user_did from auth context in all handlers

All protected web handlers now extract AuthUser from request
extensions and pass user_did to Database trait methods. The
scan_job launch_scan/run_scan functions accept user_did and
thread it through fingerprint, embedding, engagement, pile-on,
and pipeline calls.

* test: update integration tests for multi-user schema

All DB-touching integration tests now pass user_did to trait methods.
PostgreSQL tests use TEST_USER constant for user-scoped operations.

* docs: update CLAUDE.md for multi-user schema (v4)

Add multi-user schema bullet to post-MVP improvements. Update test
count to 225, Database trait method count to 18, schema version to v4.

* fix: address CodeRabbit review findings on PR #14

- Wrap SQLite v4 migration in BEGIN/COMMIT for atomicity
- Drop DEFAULT on user_did columns in Postgres migration after backfill
- Seed sweep dedupe set with user_did (DID) instead of protected_handle
- Show last_scan_at independently of notifications_cursor in status
- Return 500 errors instead of unwrap_or_default in accounts/events handlers
- Wrap background scan in catch_unwind to reset status on panic
- Append UTC offset to detected_at in Postgres event insertion
- Log warning on DID resolution failure in status command
- Scope Postgres test cleanup by user_did for amplification_events

* fix: address second round of CodeRabbit review findings on PR #14

- Fix negative UTC offset detection in Postgres event timestamp binding
- Use checked i32 cast for max_age_days in is_score_stale
- Rebuild amplification_events table in SQLite v4 migration (no DEFAULT on user_did)
- Propagate DB errors for median_engagement and pile_on in scan job

* fix: propagate DB errors from get_embedding in scan job

Previously mapped all Err to None, hiding real DB failures like
connection errors. Now Ok(None) still means "no embedding" (TF-IDF
fallback) while Err propagates and fails the scan.

* fix: thread authenticated actor handle through web scan job

The scan job was using config.bluesky_handle which could be empty or
belong to a different user in multi-user mode. Now launch_scan accepts
the actor_handle from the authenticated session, looked up via the new
get_user_handle trait method. Both fetch_recent_posts and the
amplification pipeline use the per-user handle instead of the global
config value.
